violation_type: Federal wire fraud, mail fraud, conspiracy to commit mail/wire fraud, and Hobbs Act extortion (2012 indictment; 2014 conviction on wire fraud); separately, NJ OIG's investigative report found EnCap misrepresented its landfill-closure qualifications when selected in 2000, failed to disclose that its founder's ownership stake had been substantially bought out (~$6.1M) shortly before the NJMC contract was signed, and withheld from lenders on a $212M state loan that it was simultaneously negotiating municipal PILOT agreements offering up to $450M in additional collateral
case_stage: NJ OIG investigative finding (2008), referred to the NJ Division of Criminal Justice; separately, EnCap's former president William Gauger was federally indicted (Jan. 2012) and convicted/sentenced (April 2014) on wire fraud and extortion charges arising from the same EnCap financing structure
summary: The NJ Office of the Inspector General (OIG, the agency later consolidated into the NJ Office of the State Comptroller) found that EnCap Golf Holdings misrepresented its qualifications to win a 2000 no-bid-style contract with the NJ Meadowlands Commission to cap and redevelop four Meadowlands landfills, concealed a major ownership change from NJMC, and withheld material financing information from public lenders on a $212 million state loan -- all while the project drew on roughly $460-467 million in EDA bonds, EIT/DEP loans, and BCIA bonds. OIG referred the matter to the Division of Criminal Justice. Separately, federal prosecutors later charged EnCap's president, William Gauger, with mail fraud, wire fraud, conspiracy, and Hobbs Act extortion for a scheme in which he extorted $100,000 from a financial consultant who had arranged financing tied to an EnCap-linked redevelopment deal; Gauger was convicted on one wire-fraud count and sentenced to probation in April 2014, closing out what press coverage called "the last of the federal corruption investigations" tied to the project. EnCap filed for bankruptcy in 2008 without completing the redevelopment.
citing_source: NJ Office of the Inspector General (consolidated into the NJ Office of the State Comptroller in 2010)
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by the FBI Newark Field Office's July 2011 press release and the U.S. Attorney's January 2012 indictment announcement on Gauger's extortion/fraud charges, and by NJBIZ's April 2014 report of his conviction and sentencing -- all independent of, and years after, the NJ OIG report.

dollar_amount_basis: NYC Comptroller audit finding of 'questionable/unsubstantiated payments' lacking documentation, within a larger $3,344,961 in flagged costs on a contract EDC grew from $7.5M to $73.5M via 21 change orders; an audit sampling finding, not an adjudicated loss or recoupment
violation_type: Contractor overbilling / unsubstantiated construction-management billing
summary: A NYC Comptroller audit found the Economic Development Corporation exercised almost no independent oversight of Turner Construction's facility/construction-management contract, whose value grew nearly tenfold (from $7.5M to $73.5M) through 21 change orders. Auditors identified $3.34M in flagged costs, including $1.796M in payments deemed 'inappropriate and questionable' for lack of substantiating documentation (contaminated-material disposal paid without required pre-audit, unsubstantiated excavation and elevator work, missing subcontractor price-proposal reviews on over 71% of sampled change orders). EDC disputed the findings as 'flawed and misleading'; no referral to DOI or a DA was found in the report or contemporaneous coverage.
citing_source: NYC Office of the Comptroller
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by The Real Deal ('Audit accuses city of lack of oversight in $73.5M Turner construction contract,' 2011-03-03), which reports the same $3.3M figure and the EDC dispute.

title: Audit Report on the Hewlett-Packard System Integration Contract Expenditures Associated with the Emergency Communications Transformation Program
entities: NYC Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications (DoITT); Hewlett-Packard (HP), prime system integrator
dollar_amount_basis: NYC Comptroller audit-identified billing errors on HP's time-and-materials work on the Emergency Communications Transformation Program; a separate $106M in HP's time-and-materials billings was flagged by the audit as potentially recoupable (an audit sampling/extrapolation finding, not an adjudicated or recouped loss)
violation_type: Contractor overbilling / improper time-and-materials billing practices
summary: A NYC Comptroller audit of DoITT's Emergency Communications Transformation Program (the roughly $2B citywide 911-system overhaul) found that Hewlett-Packard, the prime system integrator, billed the City using inflated consultant titles, unsupported labor hours, and unauthorized overtime, with timesheets sometimes approved as long as 885 days after the work was performed. Auditors identified $2.5 million in specific billing errors and stated the City could potentially recoup up to $106 million of HP's questioned time-and-materials billings. The Comptroller's report does not itself use the word 'fraud' and contains no referral to DOI or the Manhattan DA in the primary document, though some contemporaneous tech press used that word in headlines.
citing_source: NYC Office of the Comptroller
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by IEEE Spectrum, The Register, and GovTech coverage of the same May 2012 audit, though this entry does not adopt IEEE Spectrum's unverified 'fraud'/DA-referral characterization, which the primary audit document does not support.

title: NYC Comptroller's Office Secures $500,000+ Settlement from Construction Firms for Wage Theft and Payroll Fraud
entities: Sphinx Construction (subcontractor); D&K Construction Co.; Geomatrix Services; Gridspan Corp.; Volmar Construction (prime contractors held liable)
dollar_amount_basis: Settlement recovered by the NYC Comptroller's Bureau of Labor Law from four prime contractors, held liable for their subcontractor's prevailing-wage violations on 19 NYCDOE school construction projects, 2014-2016
violation_type: Certified payroll fraud / prevailing-wage theft
summary: The NYC Comptroller's own Bureau of Labor Law found that subcontractor Sphinx Construction omitted workers from the certified payroll reports it submitted for 19 NYCDOE public school construction projects between 2014 and 2016, concealing that those workers were not being paid the mandated prevailing wage. The Comptroller held the four prime general contractors liable for their subcontractor's violations and recovered a $516,500 settlement.
citing_source: NYC Office of the Comptroller
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by Crain's New York Business ('Comptroller Brad Lander reaches $500K settlement with construction firms over wage theft, payroll fraud,' 2023-06-13).

title: Audit Report on the New York City Housing Authority's Monitoring of Contractor Repairs
entities: NYC Housing Authority (NYCHA)
dollar_amount_basis: NYC Comptroller audit-based statistical estimate of unsubstantiated/undocumented micro-purchase repair payments (27% error rate on $55.8M sampled), which the audit separately noted could reach as much as $36.6M citywide; an audit extrapolation, not an adjudicated or recouped loss, and overlapping in subject matter with the federal bribery sweep already captured via ny-nycha-2025-final
violation_type: Contractor overbilling / unsubstantiated repair-contract payments
summary: Prompted by the February 2024 federal indictment of 70 current/former NYCHA employees for bribery and extortion in awarding no-bid repair contracts under $10,000 (already captured in this dataset via the ny-nycha-2024/2025 sweep entries), the NYC Comptroller's own audit separately examined NYCHA's documentation for those same micro-purchase repairs and found 46% of sampled purchase orders ($301,678 of $648,786 examined) lacked evidence the work was performed, extrapolating to $15.1M in unsubstantiated payments across four work categories (up to $36.6M citywide). One flagged example: $186,447 paid for 19 bathtub-surround installations in the Bronx with no supporting documentation, approved by an employee who was among those indicted. The audit states the Federal Monitor overseeing NYCHA 'made multiple referrals to law enforcement relating to potentially fraudulent activity.' Because this audit's dollar exposure substantially overlaps the existing DOJ-sourced NYCHA bribery-sweep entries, its figure is not counted toward the aggregate exposure total to avoid double-counting.
citing_source: NYC Office of the Comptroller
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by THE CITY ('Rampant Lack of Oversight Led to NYCHA Contract Corruption, Comptroller Audit Finds,' 2024-11-20) and the Bronx Times, both confirming the $36.6M figure and the link to the February 2024 indictment.

title: AFC Enterprises President and Associate Sentenced for Bribing Union Officials and Utility Representatives on NY-Area Roadway Reconstruction Projects
entities: Andrew Catapano (President, AFC Enterprises, Inc.); John Mikuszewski (engineer/consultant, Rosewood Contracting Corp.)
dollar_amount_basis: Joint criminal forfeiture ordered at sentencing (plus $50,000 combined fines and roughly $200,000 IRS restitution); underlying scheme involved about $10M in illicit proceeds and over $11M in inflated utility 'interference work' billings, 1990-2004
violation_type: Bribery of union officials and utility representatives; mail fraud; money laundering
summary: AFC Enterprises executive Andrew Catapano and consultant John Mikuszewski admitted bribing union officials to reduce required crew sizes and bribing Con Edison representatives to approve inflated 'interference work' billings on federally funded roadway reconstruction projects across the New York City area between 1990 and 2004. Originally indicted in April 2006, Catapano pleaded guilty mid-trial in December 2008 and was sentenced in July 2009. FHWA subsequently suspended and moved to debar both sentenced defendants. DOT-OIG led the investigation jointly with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York.
citing_source: U.S. DOT Office of Inspector General
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by the original U.S. Attorney's Office (EDNY) 2006 indictment press release.

title: Skanska Pays $19.6 Million and EEA Executives Indicted in Fulton Street Transit Center DBE Fraud Scheme
entities: Balu Kamat (President, Environmental Energy Associates); Carmine Desio (VP, EEA); Skanska USA Civil Northeast, Inc.
dollar_amount_basis: Civil settlement paid by prime contractor Skanska USA Civil Northeast to USDOT and MTA ($9.8M each); Kamat separately forfeited $188,000 and paid a $50,000 fine at his November 2011 sentencing
violation_type: DBE front-company/pass-through fraud; conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud
summary: Federal prosecutors charged EEA executives Balu Kamat and Carmine Desio with operating EEA as a DBE front company on the MTA's $1.4 billion Fulton Street Transit Center project, accepting a $5.2 million concrete/demolition subcontract it could not perform while prime contractor Skanska effectively self-performed the work and helped create the appearance of DBE participation. Skanska settled with USDOT and the MTA for $19.6 million the same week without admitting wrongdoing; Kamat later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to home confinement, forfeiting $188,000.
citing_source: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by Engineering News-Record (Skanska's $19.6M settlement) and DOT-OIG's own case library (Kamat sentencing).

title: Man O'Trees and Sue-Perior Concrete Owners Sentenced for DBE Fraud on Western New York Highway Projects
entities: Man O'Trees, Inc. (MOT); David Pfeiffer (MOT owner/president); Sue-Perior Concrete and Paving, Inc.; Thomas Colton (Sue-Perior majority owner/president)
dollar_amount_basis: Combined criminal fines ordered at sentencing (Man O'Trees $200,000; Pfeiffer and Colton $5,000 each); underlying ARRA/DOT-funded highway contracts affected were valued at approximately $15.5 million
violation_type: DBE pass-through/front-company fraud; conspiracy to commit mail fraud
summary: Between 2009 and 2013, general contractor Man O'Trees used Sue-Perior Concrete and Paving's DBE certification to win Western New York highway contracts partly funded by the 2009 stimulus (ARRA) and valued at roughly $15.5 million, while Man O'Trees performed the actual work itself, denying the program's benefit to a genuine disadvantaged business. Owners David Pfeiffer and Thomas Colton pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail fraud and were sentenced alongside the corporate defendant in December 2023, more than seven years after DOT-OIG and FHWA's 2016 indictment.
citing_source: U.S. DOT Office of Inspector General
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by the U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York press release on the original 2016 indictment.

title: Long Island Paving Company Owner and Employee Sentenced for Certified Payroll Fraud on FAA and Port Authority Contracts
entities: Frank Lizza (former owner, Intercounty Paving Associates, LLC); Ramon De Los Santos (former Intercounty employee); LR Safety Consultants & Construction Services, LLC; 4L Equipment Leasing, LLC
dollar_amount_basis: Joint-and-several restitution to the union benefits fund ordered at sentencing; Lizza separately owed an additional $182,119 in IRS restitution determined at a follow-up hearing
violation_type: Certified payroll fraud / false statements to FAA; diversion of union work to evade benefit-fund contributions
summary: Between 2014 and 2018, Intercounty Paving owner Frank Lizza and employee Ramon De Los Santos submitted falsified certified payrolls to the FAA and the Port Authority of NY & NJ, intentionally omitting hours worked by unionized employees of LR Safety Consultants and reassigning that work to a non-union shell company, 4L Equipment Leasing, to avoid required union benefit-fund payments. Both were sentenced in 2025 following a multi-year DOT-OIG, IRS-CI, DOL-OIG, and Port Authority-OIG investigation; FHWA moved to debar Lizza and his companies in March 2026.
citing_source: U.S. DOT Office of Inspector General
corroboration_note: Multi-agency joint investigation independently corroborated across DOT-OIG, IRS Criminal Investigation, DOL-OIG, and Port Authority-OIG filings.

title: New Jersey-Based DBE Contractor Sentenced for Kickback Scheme on the Willis Avenue Bridge Project
entities: Carol Sanzo; Sanzo, Ltd. (Cranford, NJ, DBE-certified fuel supplier)
dollar_amount_basis: Criminal forfeiture ordered at sentencing (plus an $18,000 fine); underlying DBE subcontract Sanzo used as a front was valued at approximately $6 million
violation_type: DBE pass-through/kickback fraud; conspiracy to commit wire fraud
summary: Between 2008 and 2012, Carol Sanzo used her DBE-certified fuel-supply company as a pass-through on the FHWA-funded, NYC DOT-administered Willis Avenue Bridge project, falsely claiming her firm supplied fuel while actually routing prime-contractor payments through Sanzo Ltd. to non-DBE subcontractors and retaining a kickback for herself. She pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and was sentenced to home confinement, probation, forfeiture, and a fine; FHWA later debarred her and her company for three years.
citing_source: U.S. DOT Office of Inspector General
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by the U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey press release on Sanzo's guilty plea and the subsequent FHWA debarment notice.

title: New Jersey Highway Contractor Pays $950,000 to Settle DBE False Claims Act Allegations
entities: MV Contracting, Inc. (Rahway/Colonia, NJ)
dollar_amount_basis: Civil False Claims Act settlement; $475,000 restored to FHWA
violation_type: False DBE certification / False Claims Act
summary: MV Contracting, a New Jersey highway contractor, resolved allegations that from October 2016 through April 2019 it obtained several FHWA-funded contracts set aside for Disadvantaged Business Enterprises despite knowing it did not qualify for DBE status, then submitted payment claims for that work. The company paid $950,000 to settle the civil False Claims Act allegations without admitting liability; DOT-OIG and the Port Authority of NY & NJ-OIG investigated alongside the U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey.
citing_source: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by trade press (Construction Dive, Equipment World) and DOT-OIG's own case library.

title: Pennsylvania Fuel Supplier Pays $692,000 to Settle DBE Fraud Claims on the New NY Bridge (Tappan Zee Replacement) Project
entities: Naughton Energy Corporation (Pennsylvania); Mariette Naughton (owner); Joseph Naughton (owner)
dollar_amount_basis: Settlement payment under a $3,273,600 consent judgment (balance suspended pending settlement compliance)
violation_type: DBE fraud (front-company/pass-through); False Claims Act
summary: Naughton Energy, a Pennsylvania-based, DBE-certified fuel supplier on the multibillion-dollar New NY Bridge (Tappan Zee replacement) project, misrepresented to prime contractor Tappan Zee Constructors that it was performing fuel-delivery work itself between August 2013 and January 2020, when a non-DBE subcontractor was actually doing most of the work. DOT-OIG led the investigation jointly with the New York State Inspector General, the Port Authority of NY & NJ-OIG, and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York; Naughton Energy and its owners settled for $692,000 under a $3.27 million consent judgment.
citing_source: U.S. DOT Office of Inspector General
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by the NYS Inspector General's own press release and trade press (National Law Review, GCAP Services).

title: Long Island Construction Company Owners Sentenced for DBE Fraud and Pension Fund Embezzlement Scheme
entities: Dorothy Loguidice (owner, Andrea Doreen Construction, Inc.); Michael Loguidice (owner, JCS Construction)
dollar_amount_basis: Amount forfeited to the government at sentencing; underlying scheme fraudulently obtained approximately $7.8M in DBE trucking/excavation subcontracts, and $900,000 in back taxes was separately ordered as restitution
violation_type: DBE false-certification fraud; money laundering; embezzlement of employee pension funds; tax fraud
summary: Dorothy and Michael Loguidice, operators of Long Island trucking/excavation firms Andrea Doreen Construction and JCS Construction, fraudulently certified their companies as Disadvantaged Business Enterprises to win roughly $7.8 million in federally funded highway subcontracts, while also embezzling from an employee pension fund and filing false corporate tax returns. They were sentenced to more than a year in prison, ordered to forfeit $1.1 million, and pay $900,000 in back taxes, following a DOT-OIG/FHWA investigation coordinated through the Long Island Federal Construction Fraud Task Force.
citing_source: U.S. DOT Office of Inspector General
corroboration_note: No independent second source (news archive or USAO press release) located despite a documented search; DOT-OIG's own case library is the only source found, consistent with this dataset's existing treatment of similarly aged, hard-to-verify cases (e.g. ny-nycdot-2008-01).

title: United Continental Holdings Settles SEC Charges Over Flight Route Reinstated to Benefit Port Authority Chairman
entities: United Continental Holdings, Inc.; David Samson (former Port Authority Chairman, named in the order's narrative but not a respondent in this SEC proceeding)
dollar_amount_basis: SEC civil penalty paid by United Continental Holdings, Inc. under a books-and-records/internal-controls order (separate from the $2.25M United paid under a non-prosecution agreement with the U.S. Attorney, and separate from Samson's own criminal case)
violation_type: Books-and-records and internal-accounting-controls violations (Exchange Act Sections 13(b)(2)(A)/(B)) arising from an undisclosed bribery-adjacent benefit to a public official
summary: In 2011, United reinstated a money-losing nonstop route between Newark and Columbia, SC, at the request of then-Port Authority Chairman David Samson, who wanted easier access to his South Carolina home, after United officials discussed fears that Samson could otherwise impede Port Authority approval of United's pending Newark hangar project. The SEC found United's CEO approved the route outside the airline's normal review process and that United failed to maintain accurate books and records reflecting the decision's true rationale. United settled the SEC's charges by paying a $2.4 million civil penalty; Samson separately pleaded guilty to bribery over the same scheme in a parallel DOJ case (see panynj-2016-samson-chairmans-flight).
citing_source: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by SEC press release 2016-253, the parallel DOJ/USAO-NJ non-prosecution agreement, and contemporaneous press coverage (WHYY, Courthouse News, Corporate Crime Reporter).

title: Port Authority of New York and New Jersey Charged With Failing to Disclose Legal Risks to Bondholders Financing New Jersey Roadway Projects
entities: Port Authority of New York and New Jersey
dollar_amount_basis: SEC civil penalty paid by the Port Authority
violation_type: Municipal bond disclosure fraud (Securities Act Sections 17(a)(2)/17(a)(3)) -- omission of known legal-authority risk to bondholders financing named capital roadway projects
summary: Between January 2012 and June 2014, the Port Authority issued roughly $2.3 billion in consolidated bonds that included about $1.8 billion earmarked for New Jersey state roadway projects -- the Pulaski Skyway, the Route 139 Hoboken/Conrail viaducts, the Wittpenn (Route 7) Bridge over the Hackensack River, and Route 1&9T -- even though its own in-house lawyers had privately concluded there was 'no clear path to legislative authority' to fund non-Port-Authority roadways and had flagged 'the risk of a successful challenge by the bondholders and investors.' Bond offering documents nonetheless told investors the proceeds were being used 'only for purposes for which the Port Authority is authorized by law.' The Port Authority settled by admitting the SEC's findings and paying a $400,000 civil penalty, becoming the first municipal bond issuer to admit wrongdoing in an SEC enforcement action.
citing_source: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
corroboration_note: Independently corroborated by SEC press release 2017-4, Bloomberg's Jan. 10, 2017 report, and a Chapman and Cutler LLP client alert summarizing the same admitted findings.
